opus-5.5.text:
It's been a pretty remarkable arc to watch, honestly. When I first started working on this, around the time we were building generative agents, the core intuition was that these models are trained on an enormous amount of human-written text, so in some sense they've absorbed a lot of how people talk, reason, and behave across all kinds of situations. The question was whether you could actually draw on that to produce believable behavior, not just a single plausible sentence, but an agent that wakes up, plans its day, remembers a conversation from yesterday, and acts on it.

Early on, the models were impressive but brittle. You could get a nice response to a single prompt, but the moment you needed consistency over time, a character that stays the same person across hundreds of interactions, things fell apart. So a lot of our work was building architecture around the model: memory streams, reflection, planning. The model was the engine, but you needed scaffolding to turn it into something that behaved like a coherent agent.

What's changed since then is that the models themselves have gotten much better at the things we used to have to engineer around. Longer context, better reasoning, better instruction following. So the bottleneck has shifted. It's less "can this produce believable behavior" and more "is this behavior accurate?" Believability and accuracy are different things. An agent can feel very human and still be wrong about how a specific person, or a specific population, would actually respond.

That's pushed my work toward grounding these simulations in real people. Instead of a made-up persona, you build an agent from rich data about an actual individual, like a long interview, and then measure how well it predicts that person's answers on surveys, personality measures, and behavioral experiments. That shift from plausible to measurably faithful is, I think, the most important evolution. It turns simulation from a cool demo into something that could become a real scientific and policy tool, letting us test interventions or ask "what if" questions about a society before trying them on real people.

There are still open challenges, of course. Models can flatten diversity, drifting toward a kind of average, agreeable person, and they carry the biases of their training data. But the foundation is far stronger than when we started, and I think we're just beginning to see what it makes possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the idea of simulating human behavior computationally is really old. It goes back to the fifties and sixties with people like Herbert Simon and Allen Newell, who were trying to model how people make decisions, and then later agent-based modeling in the social sciences, where you'd write down a few simple rules for how agents interact and see what emerges. Those were powerful ideas, but the agents themselves were very thin. You'd hand-code the rules, and they could only ever do the handful of things you'd thought to write down.

What changed with language models is that, for the first time, we had a model that had absorbed an enormous amount of what people actually say and do. It wasn't built to simulate people, it was built to predict text, but a huge fraction of text is people describing their lives, explaining their reasoning, arguing, reminiscing. So almost as a side effect, these models learned a lot about human behavior. And that meant you could suddenly ask an agent to react to a situation nobody had scripted in advance, and get something plausible back.

I saw this evolve in a few stages. Early on, with GPT-2 and the first version of GPT-3, you could get believable snippets. A character could say one thing that sounded human. But it fell apart over time. There was no memory, no consistency, the agent would contradict itself five minutes later. That's really what pushed us toward the generative agents work. The model gave you a good local behavior engine, but you had to build an architecture around it, memory, reflection, planning, so that behavior could stay coherent over days of simulated time and across many interacting agents. The model alone wasn't the agent. The agent was the model plus that scaffolding.

Then the models themselves got much better at long context and at following instructions, and that shifted where the hard problems were. It stopped being about whether the agent can act believably and became about whether it acts accurately, meaning, does it actually behave the way a specific real person would, or the way a population would in aggregate. That's where we moved toward grounding agents in real data, like interviewing actual people and conditioning the agent on their interviews, so you could compare the simulation against how those same people responded on surveys and experiments.

So I'd summarize the evolution as going from believable, to coherent, to accurate. And I think we're still somewhere in that third phase. The models are a remarkable foundation, but a foundation is all they are. The interesting scientific work is in what you build on top of them and in how honestly you measure the gap between the simulation and the real thing.

r002.rationale: The response credits memory, reflection, and planning scaffolding for coherent agents, but does not mention instruction tuning or connect it to reasoning about memories.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is that language models have given us a much more general foundation for representing human behavior. Traditionally, if you wanted to simulate people, you had to specify a lot of the behavior yourself: what actions they could take, what rules they would follow, and how they would respond to particular situations. That can be useful, but it’s difficult to capture the richness of everyday life that way.

With language models, you can describe a person and their situation in natural language, and the model can generate plausible behavior across a much wider range of contexts. But that doesn’t automatically give you a coherent simulation of a person. You still need ways for them to remember experiences, reflect on what those experiences mean, and use that information to plan what to do next.

And I think it’s important to separate plausibility from accuracy. A simulated person can seem very believable without actually responding the way the person you’re trying to represent would respond. So the opportunity has expanded enormously, but so has the need to evaluate what these simulations capture—and where they fall short.

r002.rationale: The response mentions agents remembering and reflecting on experiences, but does not credit instruction tuning or connect it to the generative agents work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is that language models give us a much more general foundation for representing human behavior. In traditional simulations, you often have to specify the rules yourself: what an agent can do, how it responds, and what information matters. That can be useful, but it also limits the range of behavior you can capture.

With language models, you can describe a person’s situation in natural language and get a plausible response across many different contexts. But a plausible response isn’t the same as a coherent person over time. For that, you need mechanisms for remembering experiences, reflecting on them, and using those memories to plan future actions.

So I see the evolution as moving from generating isolated responses toward building agents whose behavior has continuity. And the central question becomes how we evaluate that behavior—whether it actually captures something about people, rather than simply sounding convincing.
